'''Michael F. Crommie''' (born December 1961) is an American physicist. He is a professor of physics at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. Renowned for his research on [[condensed-matter physics]], he is a recipient of both the Newcomb-Cleveland Prize and the Davisson–Germer Prize in Atomic Physics.<ref>https://www.aaas.org/awards/newcomb-cleveland-prize/recipients</ref> Crommie currently directs the Crommie Research Group.<ref name="profile">[https://physics.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/michael-crommie Faculty profile], UC Berkeley, retrieved 2025-11-24.</ref>

==Education==
Crommie completed his undergraduate studies at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], earning a [[bachelor's degree]] in physics in 1984. He completed his doctoral studies under [[Alex Zettl]] at [[UC Berkeley]], receiving a [[Ph.D.]] in physics in 1991, and was a postdoctoral fellow at [[IBM]] under [[Don Eigler]]. In 2007, he was elected as a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Michael Crommie|url=http://www.lbl.gov/msd/investigators/investigators_all/crommie_investigator.html|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110519115449/http://www.lbl.gov/msd/investigators/investigators_all/crommie_investigator.html|archivedate=2011-05-19}}</ref>

==Research==
Crommie's research group currently uses [[scanning tunneling microscopy]] and scanning tunneling spectroscopy. Crommie is known for demonstrating the [[Quantum mirage|quantum corral]] in 1993 with Christopher Lutz and [[Don Eigler]] by using an elliptical ring of cobalt atoms on a copper surface. The ferromagnetic cobalt atoms reflected the surface electrons of the copper inside the ring into a wave pattern, as predicted by the theory of [[quantum mechanics]].
